subject: WSJ Travel: No More Airbnb Chores 🧺
body_text:
96 Plus, JetBlue goes kid-free, and American Express dilutes a hotel perk   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser             Sponsored by       Dawn Gilbertson   Say Goodbye to Those Onerous Chores at Airbnbs   Plus, JetBlue goes kid-free, and American Express dilutes a hotel perk   Greetings from my hotel balcony in Miami. This is the two-night work stay I booked with credits from the pricey Chase Sapphire Reserve card since they are use it or lose it . Happy to report the included perks, like free breakfast, $100 resort credit and a room upgrade, came through. Hope the credit covers the $6 Diet Coke I took from the minibar in a moment of deadline desperation. 

   Next week I check into a Rome hotel I booked to cash in on similar credits from the premium American Express Platinum card. It’s a one-night stay and I’m sorry to report that similar Fine Hotels & Resorts bookings will require a two-night stay to trigger the semiannual $300 lodging credit beginning next year , the credit card giant said this week. New, though: You’ll be able to use it for luxury Airbnbs. Amex already requires two-night stays for some hotels in the program and Chase has a two-night minimum.  

   In other travel news this week, United, American, Southwest and Alaska reported quarterly earnings and executives more or less repeated what they’ve been saying since the Iran war   began: Airline ticket prices are going to stay high to help cover their sky-high fuel bills and strong travel demand. 

   JetBlue launched a headline-grabbing promotion, offering its first kid-free flights. The airline partnered with adults-only cruise line Virgin Voyages for a “ Do Not Disturb” package that included seats on a chartered JetBlue flight round-trip from New York to Florida and a four-night cruise. It sold out in two hours! Yes, there were only 60 spots but JetBlue takes it as a sign of demand for something commercial airline passengers typically only dream of.  

   Waymo added two new airports to its lineup, Las Vegas and Nashville. Here’s what it’s like to use the robotaxis for airport rides .  

   Confused or concerned by the protests in Paris? Here’s a primer . 

       Airbnb retreat     ISTOCK   Airbnb turned into a verb because there’s a lot to love about the popular hotel alternative. More space, privacy, home cooking and no cookie cutter rooms or scant closet space . The list goes on.

   What travelers have come to hate, however, are chore checklists. You know, that list of duties before you check out. We’re not talking about locking up and turning off the lights.

   At some places, the to-do lists are longer than the manifestos my working mom left us on the counter after school every day. Who wants to do a deep clean at the tail end of vacation? Perhaps most irritating: the do-it-yourself cleanup is required on top of a hefty cleaning fee.

   Hotel rivals have even poked fun at the requests.

   This week, Airbnb announced a new “house rules” policy that drew raves from travelers and complaints from some hosts.

   “House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we’ve heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage,” the company said in a statement. “So we’ve redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”

   What’s out: Stripping the bed, taking trash off-site, washing or putting away dishes and other tasks that require significant effort or time. Hosts can make reasonable requests, Airbnb says, including asking that used dishes be put in the sink.

   The policy goes into effect for bookings made on or after November 20. Some Airbnb hosts aren’t happy, especially about the dirty dishes policy, and have started petitions to reverse the new policy.  

   What do you think of this new policy? Are you worried cleaning fees might go up? Send me an email at dawn.gilbertson@wsj.com or reply to this email.

   This is an edition of the WSJ Travel newsletter, a weekly source of inspiration and advice for navigating your vacations and business trips, along with the latest travel news. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       Notes From the Road ✈️     VICTOR J. BLUE/BLOOMBERG   • It isn’t your imagination. Holiday airfares are sky high .

   • Is it time to BYOBB? The mystery of the disappearing airline barf bag . 

   • 100 selfies, zero sleep: A day in the life of a Carnival cruise director.   

   • The last flight of Lufthansa’s quirkiest plane. An aviation love story from the New York Times.

From the Mediterranean and the Caribbean to Antarctica and the Galápagos, Silversea voyages are defined by immersive exploration, personalized service, all-inclusive indulgence, culinary innovation, and unmatched access to the world.   Discover More  >       Travel Math 🧮   $231.69   Southwest Airlines’ average passenger fare in the third quarter, compared with $182.56 a year ago. That’s a 27% increase.

       And We Quote 💬   “You can’t just like take a Four-Seasons room, copy the room, put it in a Motel 6 and expect it to be Four Seasons.”

   — United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, on smaller airlines’ plans to join United and other big airlines in wooing premium travelers .

       You Have Thoughts 🤔   …on taking public transportation to or from New York airports : 

   • “Loved your article about traveling from JFK to Midtown Manhattan for the amazing price of $16. A dozen years ago, my daughter and I flew to New York for a show and some touristing. We took the subway to Harlem and caught a bus to LaGuardia from there. I was used to taking express buses in Charlotte, N.C., so was very comfortable with public transport. A security guard at a CVS showed us where it stopped. Total cost of the commute? Less than $5 each. Would I do it again? Absolutely! The trick is traveling light and paying attention to your surroundings.” — Ellen Frank, South Carolina  

   (Responses have been condensed and edited.) 

       Cheers and Jeers 🤷   Cheers to American’s new automatic seat mover feature. For a mid-November flight, I got an alert this week that it moved me to a better aisle seat in the extra legroom section. The alert came in as I was boarding another American flight and I mistakenly thought they had changed that very good bulkhead seat. 

   Jeers to the self-checkout stations at airport sundry stores. They are supposed to speed things up but instead you’re asked a series of annoying questions. Bags? Charity donation? Rewards program? All I want is my overpriced protein shake.

       In My Carry-on 👜     SOUTHWEST AIRLINES   Nandika Suri, the new vice president of Southwest Airlines’ frequent flier program, brings homemade protein balls on the road with her.

   She saw a recipe online and adjusted it so there’s less sugar. The typical ingredients: peanut butter or almond butter, chia seeds, flax seeds, oatmeal and shredded coconut.

   “I think I’m the only one that likes it [that way] so when I make it for other people I put in chocolate chips and cranberries.”

   She packs as many as a dozen in a reusable container from Farmers Fridge, her airport vending machine go-to for a chia pudding fix.
